name: examples/markdown/01-kitchen-sink.md slide 2
why: A blank line between numbered items. The hand-written walk ends the list at the blank and starts again at the number the deck wrote, so `7.` becomes the first number of a second list; CommonMark keeps one list whose numbering carries on. The walk also gives an item whose predecessor carried no number its own number again, which draws `1. 2. 3.` correctly by coincidence and `1. 1. 1.` as three numbers.

name: examples/markdown/05-steps.md slide 3
why: Two bullets with a blank line between them: two shapes here and one list there. The slide says so — "one click opens the step and the second shape joins it" — so switching parsers makes this page wrong unless the sentence is rewritten.

name: examples/markdown/06-tables.md slide 2
why: A code span written with two backticks around one. The hand-written pattern cannot see a run longer than one and matches the pair inside it, so the cell draws four runs of punctuation; CommonMark reads the two-backtick span as the code it is.

name: examples/markdown/06-tables.md slide 4
why: A row with more cells than the header has. The hand-written table keeps the fourth cell; CommonMark draws the row as far as the header goes, which is what this deck and the README both say a ragged row does.

name: examples/markdown/09-inline-markup.md slide 1
why: An emphasis delimiter that opens and never closes. The hand-written walk pairs it with a pair three lines later, so a paragraph about unclosed emphasis is drawn in bold and the code span after it is split down the middle; CommonMark leaves the `**` as the characters it is and reads the code span whole. This is the difference the hand-written parser was written to have.

name: examples/markdown/09-inline-markup.md slide 2
why: Emphasis inside a link's label. The hand-written link pattern takes the label as raw text, so a link written `[**heading**](…)` draws a pair of asterisks on the slide; CommonMark keeps the emphasis and the link, which is what a reader sees in every other renderer.

name: slidev: fence indented four spaces, closed flush slide 1
why: Four spaces of indentation is a code block in CommonMark and a paragraph here, so a fence written that way is drawn as characters on the slide.

name: slidev: delimiter inside an indented code block slide 1
why: The same rule as above, for an indented `---`: a code block there and a paragraph with the dashes on it here.

name: slidev: fence inside a comment slide 1
why: The refusal is the same one and the comment it quotes is not. The hand-written prose pass reads the fences inside the comment as a code block, so it quotes `<!-- -->`; league quotes the whole comment, which is what the author wrote and what has to be found in the deck to be fixed.

name: slidev: lone carriage return slide 1
why: A lone carriage return is a line ending to league and not to this library: one line of text here, two paragraphs there.

name: slidev: fence nested in a list slide 1
why: A fence indented under a bullet: a code block after the list here, words inside the bullet there, because a shape nested in a list item has nowhere of its own to be drawn.
